Session plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Advisors leave ready to lead a real conversation with their advisory group of seven or eight on any topic: something in the news, something going on at school, a question students raised, or the day after a grade talk. They work on opening with what students think, helping them zero in on one thing, rolling with pushback and quiet, and what to do if something heavy comes up. The relationship carries the conversation.

Materials

  • Scenario cards if you break into clusters, one per cluster (the four on the slide)
  • One printed conversation guide per advisor, as an example (Vaping and Your Brain works well)

Flow

  1. 6 minOpening: an advisory that fell flat, and one that went well
  2. 6 minWhy scripts flop, and what the relationship does
  3. 5 minOpen with what they think: five ways in
  4. 2 minTell a story
  5. 4 minRoll with it: pushback and quiet
  6. 10 minYour turn: talk through real scenarios, as a whole group or in clusters
  7. 3 minIf something heavy comes up, and one thing to try

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Twenty minutes: the opening, both prompts (4), why scripts flop, first slide only (3), five ways in (3), roll with it (3), clusters, one scenario (5), one thing to try (2).

Before you present
Model what you're teaching.

Run this talk the way you want advisors to run advisory. Ask before you tell, take their pushback without defending yourself, and follow a good tangent. A lecture about not lecturing would undo the point.

Curiosity is the skill.

Most advisors are quiet people, and that's fine. Say it plainly: the skill is being curious about these particular kids. The advisors who already know their group have the head start.

Keep it moving.

Long silences rarely work with high schoolers. Teach advisors to lower the stakes and keep going: ask about "people your age," go thumbs up or down, or say what they think themselves.

Let the critics in.

Some advisors will say this is touchy-feely or that their kids won't talk. Treat it the way you'd want them to treat a student who says it's cringe: "Fair. What would make it work in your room?"

The safety floor stays the same.

Something heavy in advisory gets the same response as anywhere else: thank them, keep it short in the group, check in after, and walk them to a counselor that day. Talking it through once in a scenario means it isn't new when it happens.

Bring your own story.

The opening asks faculty to share an advisory that fell flat, so go first with one of your own, a little embarrassing and true. It gives everyone permission to be imperfect at this.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Many ways in.

Some students think out loud, and some think first and talk later. Thumbs, a word on a scrap of paper, or a side conversation after advisory all count as joining in.

Families talk about these topics differently.

In some homes vaping, sex or mental health are never discussed; in others, faith shapes the answer. A student who goes quiet may be respecting home. Leave room, and never ask what their family thinks.

Who gets heard.

The loudest student is one voice. Advisors can widen it with "Anyone see it differently?" and by noticing who hasn't had a turn, without putting anyone on the spot.

Language.

English learners can answer with a word in any language, a gesture, or a number from 1 to 10. Slower turns help everyone.

Neurodivergent students.

Some students need the question twice, or a minute to think, or a concrete example. Some will go deep on one detail. That's still the conversation.

The topic may be personal.

For any talk, assume someone in the room is living it: a parent who drinks, a friend who vapes, stress that won't switch off. Keep questions about "people our age" so nobody has to out themselves.

What the research says

In a meta-analysis of 207 school drug prevention programs, interactive programs that got students talking with each other worked better than lecture-style programs that delivered information.

Tobler et al., Journal of Primary Prevention, 2000

The original D.A.R.E. program, built on adults delivering a message, had near-zero effect on later drug use across controlled studies.

West & O'Neal, American Journal of Public Health, 2004

Adolescents are especially sensitive to status and respect. Messages that treat them as capable and invite their judgment work better than ones that tell them what to do.

Yeager, Dahl & Dweck, Perspectives on Psychological Science, 2018

Eighth graders who read about food companies manipulating teens chose healthier snacks the next day, while a standard nutrition lesson made no difference.

Bryan et al., PNAS, 2016

Teacher-student relationship quality is linked to student engagement and achievement, and the link to engagement is stronger in secondary school than in elementary.

Roorda, Koomen, Spilt & Oort, Review of Educational Research, 2011

Students engage more when teachers ask for their views, explain the why, and accept negative feelings without pushing back, and teachers can learn these habits in short trainings.

Reeve & Cheon, Educational Psychologist, 2021

When a helper argues for change, people tend to argue back for the other side. Open questions and reflecting back what you heard keep the other person doing the thinking.

Miller & Rollnick, Motivational Interviewing, 3rd ed., 2013
